listenings.text: I've been training people at six in the morning for about ten years now. Most of my early clients are busy people: managers, doctors, parents. They tell me the same thing. After work, they're too tired, and there's always a meeting or a problem at home. But at six a.m., nothing can interrupt them. My advice for beginners is simple. Don't start with seven days a week. Start with three. I've been doing this long enough to know that people who try to change everything in one week usually stop in the second. Be consistent, not heroic.

For the last five years, my team has been studying how sleep affects energy and mood at work. And the results are very clear. People who sleep less than six hours a night make more mistakes and feel more stressed, even when they think they're fine. The problem is that sleep-deprived people get used to it. They stop noticing that they're worn out. So, is it bad to wake up at five? Not at all, if you go to bed early enough. My main advice is boring, but it works: go to bed and wake up at the same time every day. Your body loves a routine.

I have two kids and a full-time job, so for years I was always in a hurry. I felt I never had a minute for myself. Then, about a year ago, I started waking up one hour before everyone else. I've been doing it ever since. I make coffee, I go for a thirty-minute walk, and I read a few pages of a book. That's it. Nothing special. But when my family wakes up, I'm calm, and I'm ready. The hardest part? Honestly, it's going to bed early when there's a good series on TV. I've been learning to say: one episode, and that's it.

paras: Hannah is a lawyer in Chicago, and for the last three years, she has been waking up at five every morning. Before her kids get up, she works out, reads for twenty minutes and plans her day. “It’s the only time nobody needs me,” she says. She is part of a large group of people, often called the 5 a.m. Club, who believe that the first hours of the day are the most productive.

But is it really a good idea for everybody? Sleep scientists have been studying this for years, and their answer is: it depends. Some people are natural early birds. Others are night owls, and their bodies work better later in the day. If a night owl wakes up at five, she will probably feel worn out by the afternoon. And if you wake up early but still go to bed at midnight, you become sleep-deprived, and that is bad for your health.

So what is the secret? According to the experts, it is not the hour on the clock. It is being consistent: going to bed and waking up at the same time, even on weekends, and sleeping seven or eight hours. Willpower helps you get up, but sleep is what helps you recharge. Hannah agrees. “I’ve been going to bed at nine-thirty since I started,” she says. “Without that, I couldn’t stick to it.”
